areas.proof_note: Scheduled, source-linked reporting is the analytics agent pattern: a plain-language digest on schedule, unattended. Built for a marketing team, not for month end.

areas.name: Data quality and alerts
areas.pain: A sync stalled on Tuesday and nobody noticed until the numbers looked odd on Friday.
areas.hook: Still finding out a sync broke when the dashboard looks wrong days later?

services.name: Freshness and row-count checks on every load
services.what: Each table carries its last-loaded time and expected row range. A load that is late, empty or far from the usual volume is flagged in Slack or Teams the same morning.
services.human: A person decides whether to rerun or wait; the check only alerts.

services.name: Expired tokens and stalled connections caught early
services.what: API tokens, OAuth grants and SFTP logins to each platform are tested on schedule, with non-expiring auth flows where the platform allows it, so the sync does not silently stop after a refresh.
services.human: A person reconnects the platform; the system only alerts.

services.name: Bad rows quarantined with the reason
services.what: Deterministic checks on every row: required fields, valid dates, totals that add up, keys that exist. Rows that fail are held in a quarantine table with the failed rule, and the rest load.
services.human: Your team clears the quarantine; a rule is never relaxed without your sign-off.

services.name: Numbers out of range flagged before sending
services.what: A total that moves more than its usual range day on day, a customer that appears twice, a negative stock figure: flagged with the rows behind it before the report goes out.
services.human: You choose which flags hold the report and which only annotate it.

services.name: Data quality scorecard per source
services.what: A Power BI page showing, per platform, when it last loaded, how many rows failed which rule, and how long the quarantine has been open. Built on the freshness and quarantine tables above.
services.human: The data owner decides what to fix first.

services.name: Closed periods still reproduce after changes
services.what: Customer, SKU and price dimensions keep their history, and every stored procedure has a regression test over a frozen month, so a report rerun for a closed period returns the same figures after a change to the pipeline.
services.human: A failed test blocks the release until you accept the new figures in writing.

areas.proof_note: Root-cause debugging in that retailer’s pipeline found voided shipments and multi-cause inflation; these checks come from that. A US retailer’s finance team, not BI.

areas.name: Documents into the same tables
areas.pain: Supplier invoices and scanned PDFs never make it into the numbers.
areas.hook: Still leaving the paperwork out of the numbers because it only exists as scans?

services.name: Invoices and scans extracted into the dataset
services.what: Supplier invoices, delivery notes, scanned PDFs and HTML exports extracted by text and vision models into the same validated tables, with deterministic checks after the model.
services.human: Nothing is written until it passes the gate. A person clears the queue; the pipeline never guesses.

services.name: Entity resolution built for OCR noise
services.what: “ACME Ltd” and “Acme Limited” resolved to one supplier with an escalating matcher instead of one similarity threshold.
services.human: Low-confidence matches are confirmed by a person once, then remembered.

services.name: Inbox and shared-drive intake for documents
services.what: Attachments arriving in a shared mailbox, a SharePoint or Google Drive folder, or a Dropbox upload are picked up on arrival by n8n, deduplicated and handed to the extraction pipeline with their source recorded.
services.human: You choose the folders and mailboxes; nothing is moved or deleted at source.

services.name: Documents matched to orders and payments
services.what: Each extracted invoice or delivery note is joined to the order, shipment and payment it belongs to in the fact tables, so cost per order and unmatched paperwork become queries, not a hunt.
services.human: Unmatched documents are listed for a person; nothing is force-matched.

services.name: Exceptions queue with the failed rule shown
services.what: A small web screen built on Next.js and FastAPI: the scan on the left, the extracted fields and the rule it failed on the right. Staff correct, resubmit, and the correction is logged.
services.human: Only a person can override a failed rule, and the override is recorded with their name.

areas.proof_note: 412 records, 0 validation errors with an 8-tier fuzzy resolver and a hard validation gate. Tournament data, not operations paperwork.

areas.name: Spreadsheets that run operations
areas.pain: One person owns the master spreadsheet, and the business stops when they are on holiday.
areas.hook: Still running operations from one master spreadsheet that only one person understands?

services.name: Sheet formulas rebuilt as SQL, then matched
services.what: The lookups, pivots and formulas in the master workbook are mapped and rebuilt as stored procedures over the same inputs, then run beside the sheet until both agree, tab by tab.
services.human: The sheet’s owner signs off each tab. The workbook is not retired until they do.

services.name: Excel stays, but it reads the database
services.what: The workbooks people will not give up are connected to the SQL views with refreshable Power Query connections, so the formulas stay, the pasted-in data goes, and a refresh replaces the retyping.
services.human: The workbook owner keeps the workbook; only the data tabs change.

services.name: Manual inputs through a form, not cells
services.what: The handful of numbers someone types in each week, targets, headcount, adjustments, are entered through a short form that writes to a table with validation and a who-and-when stamp.
services.human: You decide who may enter which figures; every entry is traceable to a person.

services.name: Google Sheets and Airtable as governed sources
services.what: The Sheets and Airtable bases teams already fill in are read into staging on schedule by API, with locked columns, type checks and a change log, so they become inputs to the pipeline rather than the pipeline itself.
services.human: Sheet owners keep editing rights; a row that fails a type check is flagged, not dropped.

services.name: Macros and VBA replaced by scheduled jobs
services.what: The VBA macros and manual refresh buttons that only run on one laptop become scheduled jobs on a server, logged, with the same outputs and an alert when a run fails.
services.human: The macro’s author checks the first runs against the old output.

areas.proof_note: Staging and stored procedures, every transformation inspectable in SQL, parity-audited before cutover. The legacy there was a retailer’s system, not a spreadsheet.

areas.name: Hosting, access and residency
areas.pain: Security asked where the data lives, and the answer is a laptop and a trial account.
areas.hook: Still unable to tell security where the reporting data actually lives?

services.name: SQL Server and pipeline on EU-resident servers
services.what: The database, n8n and the scheduled jobs deployed on a hardened server in the EU or on your own Azure tenant: key-only SSH, firewall, services bound to loopback, backups tested by restoring them.
services.human: You sign off the architecture sketch and the residency rules before the build starts.

services.name: Self-hosted models for documents that cannot leave
services.what: Open-weight text and vision models run on your own GPU server for the extraction steps, so invoices, contracts and personal data in the pipeline never reach a third-party API. Extraction accuracy on your documents is measured before cutover.
services.human: You decide which document types may use a hosted API and which may not.

services.name: Who can see what, written down and enforced
services.what: Database roles, Power BI workspaces and row-level security mapped to your Microsoft 365 or Google groups, reviewed with you, and exported as a list security can read.
services.human: Your admin grants and removes access; I document and check it.

services.name: Backups, restore drills and a runbook
services.what: Nightly database backups kept off the server, a restore tested on a schedule, and a short runbook your team can follow when I am not there.
services.human: You choose the retention period and who holds the keys.

services.name: Audit log of every load and override
services.what: Every pipeline run, its row counts and every manual override logged to a table with who, what and when, with row-level logging only on the tables you name, so an auditor’s question about a number has an answer.
services.human: The log is append-only; you set how long it is kept.

areas.proof_note: The analytics agent runs on a hardened EU-resident server: key-only SSH, dual firewall, fail2ban, loopback-only services. A marketing team’s agent, not a BI stack.

name: SaaS and software companies
question_lede: A working product, paying users, and an AI feature that is still a prompt in a notebook.

areas.name: Slow inference in production
areas.pain: It worked in the notebook; in the product the request hangs until the gateway gives up.
areas.hook: Still shipping an AI feature that works in the demo and times out in production?

services.name: Queued jobs and polling instead of held requests
services.what: A FastAPI job API and a GPU worker as separate services: jobs are queued and polled, not held open until they time out, and the expensive part scales on its own. Your Next.js app shows progress.
services.human: Every job is tracked from upload to result with status and timing, so your team can audit a run.

services.name: Self-hosted models where data must stay
services.what: Open-weight models on your own GPUs, on RunPod or a hardened EU-resident server, served by the same job API and worker, so an enterprise security review does not stall on a third-party API.
services.human: You sign off the architecture sketch before the build starts.

services.name: Typed contracts on every boundary
services.what: Model output validated into a fixed Pydantic schema before the UI sees it, so a new edge case fails loudly in one place instead of shipping as a hotfix. Added to the feature you already run.
services.human: Your team owns the schema; changes are reviewed like any code.

services.name: Streaming so users see progress, not a spinner
services.what: Server-sent events from the FastAPI job API to your React or Next.js front end, with partial results and step names as they happen, so a long job reads as work in progress, not a hang.
services.human: Your designers decide what the user sees at each step.

services.name: GPU workers that scale to zero
services.what: The worker runs on RunPod serverless: it starts when the queue fills and stops when it empties, with a warm pool sized to your traffic so the first job of the morning is not the slowest.
services.human: You set the spend ceiling and the warm pool size.

services.name: Retries, timeouts and dead-letter handling
services.what: Jobs that fail at the model or the worker are retried with backoff, capped, then parked in a dead-letter queue with the error, so nothing silently disappears and nothing loops forever.
services.human: Your on-call engineer owns the dead-letter queue; no failed job is deleted automatically.

areas.proof_note: A live three-service SaaS: Next.js, FastAPI and a RunPod GPU worker, ~110 s per job, queued and polled. Built for dental clinics.

areas.name: Agent prototype rescue
areas.pain: The agent demo works twice and loops on the third run, and nobody can say why.
areas.hook: Still demoing an agent that loops on the third run?

services.name: Prototype rebuilt with one typed shared state
services.what: The prototype rebuilt as a LangGraph graph with one typed shared state instead of message passing, Pydantic-validated outputs at every agent boundary, a QA agent, and retries with correction capped at two attempts.
services.human: Outputs that fail QA twice are parked for a person with the reason. Nothing loops or fails silently.

services.name: Provider-agnostic model layer
services.what: Models swappable per agent, Claude, OpenAI, Gemini or an open-weight model, without touching orchestration. The typed state and the QA gate stay the same whichever model runs.
services.human: Your team chooses models per step and can change them any time.

services.name: Tool calls made safe and idempotent
services.what: Every tool the agent can call gets a typed input schema, a read-only or write flag, an idempotency key and a budget, so a retried step cannot send twice or charge twice.
services.human: You set the budget per run; a tool that exceeds it stops the run with the reason.

services.name: Graph replay tests with recorded runs
services.what: Real runs recorded as fixtures and replayed in pytest with model calls stubbed, checking routing, state transitions and tool calls rather than output quality, so a refactor of the graph fails in CI, not in a demo. Output scoring lives in the eval set.
services.human: Your team decides which runs become fixtures and when they are refreshed.

services.name: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints inside the graph
services.what: Named pause points in the LangGraph graph where the run waits for a person: approve, edit the state, or reject with a reason. The run resumes from the checkpoint, not from the start.
services.human: Your product team decides which steps need a person and who that person is.

services.name: Run traces your support team can read
services.what: Every agent step logged with inputs, outputs, model, tokens and time, viewable per run in a simple page, so “why did it say that” is a lookup rather than a reproduction.
services.human: You decide retention and who may open a trace that contains customer data.

areas.proof_note: 6 agents, one typed shared state, Pydantic at every boundary, pytest over the graph, QA retries capped at two. Built for lead research.

areas.name: Document intelligence in your product
areas.pain: Users upload PDFs and scans and the feature returns free text that breaks the UI.
areas.hook: Still returning free text from uploads and fixing the UI with hotfixes?

services.name: Uploads extracted into your schema, then validated
services.what: PDFs, scans and messy uploads extracted by text and vision models into your schema, with deterministic validation after the model: the model proposes, rules decide. Built into your existing app and API.
services.human: Records that fail the gate are queued for your team or your users to resolve.

services.name: Entity resolution instead of one threshold
services.what: An escalating matcher, exact to fuzzy in tiers, built for OCR noise, so names, references and codes from a scan resolve reliably against the records already in the user’s account.
services.human: Confidence thresholds are set with you and visible to users where it matters.

services.name: Upload flow with progress and a review screen
services.what: Drag-and-drop upload in your Next.js app, a queued extraction job with progress, then a side-by-side screen where the user confirms or corrects each field before it is saved.
services.human: Nothing is saved to the user’s account until they confirm it.

services.name: Corrections fed back into the eval set
services.what: Every field a user corrects is stored with the original document and added to the extraction eval set as a regression case, so accuracy is measured against real corrections rather than a demo set.
services.human: You decide which customers’ documents may be used and how long they are kept.

services.name: Tables, handwriting and multi-page documents
services.what: Line-item tables, handwritten fields, stamps and documents that run over several pages handled as their own cases with their own checks, instead of one prompt that works on the clean sample.
services.human: You bring the ugly real documents; the acceptance set is agreed before the build.

services.name: Per-customer document layouts mapped once
services.what: A customer’s recurring layout, their supplier’s invoice or their own form, is mapped once and stored per layout, so the second document of that kind extracts with the same checks and no new prompt.
services.human: A new layout is confirmed by the user before the mapping is saved.

areas.proof_note: 412 records from HTML, PDFs and scans, 0 validation errors, with an 8-tier resolver and a hard gate. Tournament data, not a SaaS product.

areas.name: From notebook to shipped feature
areas.pain: The prompt works in a notebook, and nobody owns getting it into the product.
areas.hook: Still carrying an AI feature as a prompt in a notebook, six months on?

services.name: Feature scoped from the notebook, with acceptance set
services.what: A week with your notebook and your real data: the feature defined as inputs, outputs and failure cases, an acceptance set of real examples agreed, and an architecture sketch your team can build or hand to me.
services.human: Your product owner signs off the acceptance set; it is the definition of done.

services.name: LLM pipeline with structured outputs, behind a flag
services.what: The prompt becomes a pipeline in your codebase: typed inputs, cached context, model call, schema-validated output, fallback when validation fails. Summarise a ticket, classify a record, pull fields from free text, draft a reply. Shipped behind a feature flag, eval set in CI.
services.human: Your team turns the flag on per customer; nothing reaches a user you did not choose.

services.name: Search and answers over each customer’s records
services.what: Retrieval over each customer’s own documents and records in your Postgres, with per-tenant isolation, citations in every answer, and a refusal path when the answer is not in their data. Built into your product, not a chatbot bolted on.
services.human: Your team sets what may be indexed per plan; users see the sources behind every answer.

services.name: Vision features over user photos and screenshots
services.what: Photo and screenshot inputs handled by a vision model with the output validated into your schema: damage reports, receipts, product shots, UI screenshots. Queued through the job API when the model is slow.
services.human: The acceptance set of real photos is agreed with you before the build.

areas.proof_note: LeadForge runs in production: Pydantic-validated outputs at every boundary, pytest over the graph, streamed into Next.js. Built for lead research.

areas.name: Evals, QA and inference cost
areas.pain: Nobody can say whether the last prompt change made it better, and the API bill doubled.
areas.hook: Still changing prompts by feel and finding out from the invoice?

services.name: Eval set built from real inputs and outputs
services.what: A few hundred real inputs from your product, labelled with your team, scored automatically on each change: exact fields by rules, judgement calls by a model grader you have checked against humans.
services.human: Your team labels the set; a grader is trusted only after it agrees with them.

services.name: Prompt and model changes gated in CI
services.what: Every prompt, schema or model change runs the eval set in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, with the score diff posted on the pull request, so a regression is seen before merge, not after release.
services.human: Your reviewers decide whether a score drop is acceptable; the gate only reports.

services.name: Live outputs sampled and scored daily
services.what: A sample of yesterday’s production outputs scored each night against the same eval rules and grader, per model and per tenant, with an alert in Slack when the score drifts below the floor you set.
services.human: An alert opens a review by your team; nothing is rolled back or switched automatically.

services.name: Prompt caching and model routing to cut cost
services.what: Stable context cached so it is not paid for on every call, cheap models for easy cases and strong models for hard ones, with the routing rule explicit and the cost per request logged.
services.human: You set the quality floor from the eval set; cost is cut only above it.

services.name: Inference cost per tenant, in your database
services.what: Tokens, model, latency and cost written per request and per tenant into your Postgres or SQL Server, with a Power BI or Metabase view, so AI pricing and plan limits rest on numbers.
services.human: Your finance lead decides the plan limits; the system only measures and alerts.

services.name: Rate limits, budgets and kill switch per tenant
services.what: Per-tenant request limits, a daily spend ceiling and a switch that turns a feature off for one customer or everyone, enforced in the FastAPI layer, so an abusive script cannot run up the bill overnight.
services.human: Your on-call engineer holds the switch; limits are set by you per plan.

areas.proof_note: Prompt caching cut per-image inference cost by 78%; every output carries its QA verdict and the rule. An education brand’s ads, not a SaaS.

areas.name: Support tickets and in-app help
areas.pain: The support queue grows with every new customer, and the docs answer half of it.
areas.hook: Still answering the same ten questions in Intercom while the queue grows?

services.name: Tickets triaged and routed with a reason
services.what: New tickets in Intercom, Zendesk, HubSpot or Front classified by topic, urgency and plan through their APIs, tagged and routed to the right queue, with the reason written on the ticket.
services.human: Anything tagged as outage, billing dispute or legal goes straight to a person.

services.name: Replies drafted from your docs and the account
services.what: A draft reply built from your help centre, release notes and the customer’s account and recent events in your database, with the sources shown to the agent beside the draft.
services.human: A support agent edits and sends every reply. Nothing goes to a customer unreviewed.

services.name: In-app help assistant with ticket handoff
services.what: A help assistant inside your product over your help centre and release notes, that cites what it used, says when it does not know, and opens a ticket with the conversation attached when it hands off.
services.human: The assistant never changes account settings or billing; those actions go to a person.

services.name: Bug reports turned into structured issues
services.what: Tickets that describe a bug become a Linear or Jira issue with steps, plan, browser and account ID filled from the ticket fields and the customer record, linked back to the conversation.
services.human: An engineer confirms the issue before it enters the sprint; duplicates are suggested, not merged.

services.name: Weekly support digest: what customers are asking
services.what: A scheduled summary of the week’s tickets by topic, new versus recurring, and the questions the docs did not answer, posted to Slack with links to the tickets behind each line.
services.human: The support lead decides what gets a doc update or a product change.

areas.proof_note: The analytics agent reasons over 4 live integrations and posts a source-linked digest to Slack on schedule. Marketing numbers, not support tickets.

areas.name: Billing, product and revenue data
areas.pain: Stripe, the CRM and the product database each report a different MRR.
areas.hook: Still explaining to the board why Stripe and the CRM disagree on MRR?

services.name: Stripe, CRM and product data into one warehouse
services.what: Stripe or Chargebee, HubSpot or Salesforce, and your product Postgres loaded through their APIs into SQL Server or Postgres staging, then stored procedures building customer, subscription and usage fact tables, every transformation inspectable in SQL.
services.human: Your finance lead signs off a parity audit against the current MRR sheet before cutover.

services.name: MRR, churn and payouts reconciled line by line
services.what: Subscriptions, invoices, refunds and Stripe payouts matched line by line, with proration, currency and failed payments handled explicitly, so MRR, churn and cash agree and the differences are listed.
services.human: Finance reviews the listed mismatches; nothing is averaged away or auto-adjusted.

services.name: Usage metering that matches what you bill
services.what: Product events from your database, Segment or PostHog aggregated into per-tenant usage tables and checked against the quantities on the Stripe invoice, so overage and plan limits are billed from the same number.
services.human: Billing changes are made by your team; the system reports the difference.

services.name: Board metrics in Power BI, refreshed nightly
services.what: MRR, net revenue retention, churn, activation and support load as a Power BI or Metabase model on the fact tables, refreshed nightly, with each metric’s definition written beside it.
services.human: Founders and finance agree each definition once; changes are reviewed like code.

services.name: Morning product and revenue digest in Slack
services.what: An agent reads the fact tables, Stripe and your product analytics overnight and posts one short message each morning: signups, activations, churn events and failed payments, every number linked to its source.
services.human: The team reads it. The agent changes nothing in Stripe or the product.

areas.proof_note: Staging, stored procedures and fact tables in SQL Server, 68,890 orders reconciled across 25 audited columns. A retailer’s fulfilment data, not SaaS billing.

areas.name: Enterprise and self-hosted deployments
areas.pain: The enterprise deal is stuck in security review over where the AI feature sends data.
areas.hook: Still losing enterprise deals in security review over the AI feature’s data flow?

services.name: Single-tenant deployment in the customer’s cloud
services.what: Your AI feature’s API, worker and models packaged with Docker and deployed as one tenant into the customer’s AWS, Azure or Hetzner account, nothing leaving their network. Delivered with a written data flow: what goes where, under which terms, for their questionnaire.
services.human: Your team and the customer’s security lead sign off the data flow before deployment.

services.name: Per-tenant isolation, region pinning and retention
services.what: Each tenant’s documents, embeddings and model outputs under their own keys and schema, pinned to an EU or US region, retention and deletion per contract, a deletion job that proves what it removed, and the data flow written down for questionnaires.
services.human: You decide which tenants are pinned where; deletion runs only on a recorded request.

services.name: Bring-your-own-model for enterprise tenants
services.what: Tenants that insist on their own Azure OpenAI, Bedrock or Vertex account plug in their endpoint and keys per tenant, with the same schema validation and evals running against it.
services.human: You decide which plans get this; the tenant’s keys are stored only in their config.

services.name: Audit log of every model call, per tenant
services.what: Every model call recorded per tenant: who triggered it, which provider and region served it, what data left your network and when it is deleted, exportable as CSV or over your API for the customer’s compliance team.
services.human: You decide which fields the export carries; it is released only on the customer’s request.

services.name: MCP server over your product API
services.what: An MCP server over your existing public API, so a customer’s Claude or other assistant can read and act in your product, with per-tenant OAuth scopes, read-only or write flags per tool, and every call logged.
services.human: Your team chooses which endpoints become tools; write tools are off by default per tenant.

areas.proof_note: A hardened Hetzner VPS chosen for EU residency: key-only SSH, firewall, fail2ban, loopback-only services; MCP tools over 4 APIs. A marketing agent, not SaaS.

areas.name: Customer onboarding and data import
areas.pain: Every new customer brings a competitor’s export, and someone maps it into your schema by hand.
areas.hook: Still onboarding every new customer by hand from a competitor’s CSV?

services.name: Competitor exports mapped into your schema
services.what: CSV, XLSX and JSON exports from the tools your customers leave, and the PDFs they bring, mapped into your schema: a model proposes the column mapping, rules validate every row, and the import stops at the gate with the reason.
services.human: Your onboarding team confirms the mapping; rejected rows go to a review list, never silently dropped.

services.name: Import as a queued job with a report
services.what: Large files run as a queued job in your FastAPI backend with progress in your Next.js app, and a downloadable report of which rows were imported, skipped or need a fix, so a big file does not time out a browser request.
services.human: The customer or your onboarding team reviews the report before the import is committed.

services.name: Parity check before the customer goes live
services.what: Imported records counted and compared field by field against the source export, with every difference listed in a report the customer can open, so they switch over on evidence rather than a sample.
services.human: The customer signs off the parity report; nothing in the old system is touched.

services.name: Duplicates matched on import, flagged not merged
services.what: Imported contacts, products or accounts matched against records the tenant already has, escalating from exact to fuzzy, so a migration does not create a second copy of every customer. Likely pairs are shown side by side.
services.human: A person decides each flagged pair; nothing is merged automatically.

areas.proof_note: 68,890 orders loaded through staging and reconciled column by column against the legacy system before cutover. A retailer’s fulfilment data, not a SaaS import.
